title: Manufactured Urgency Is Not the Same as Discipline
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Zambrano, a former big-tech engineer, interrogates the popular productivity advice to manufacture urgency, setting self-imposed deadlines ahead of real ones, by asking whether it is sustainable or simply a disguised path to burnout. Drawing on self-determination theory, he argues manufactured urgency typically disguises controlled motivation, acting to avoid guilt, shame, or a threat to identity, as autonomous motivation, which is what makes it psychologically costly over time: the stress response the technique creates has no natural end point the way a real deadline does. He traces this back to his own school-age habit of treating every task as urgent because his identity was tied to being the smart kid, and connects it to the physiology of chronic stress, noting that unlike animals, humans keep their alarm on even after a perceived threat passes. Zambrano's proposed fix is not abandoning self-imposed deadlines but reframing their purpose and spacing them: choosing constraints attached to real motivations, avoiding deadline pile-ups across unrelated life domains, and building in recovery gaps so stress can return to baseline before the next self-imposed push.
points: Zambrano's key psychological claim, drawn from self-determination theory, is that manufactured urgency often disguises controlled motivation as autonomous motivation, which is what makes it unsustainable.
He distinguishes real deadlines, which give the brain a signal to stop, from self-manufactured ones, which can leave stress with virtually no end when stacked across multiple unrelated life domains.
His personal example, needing to keep being the smart kid as a student, demonstrates how manufactured urgency frequently masks an identity threat rather than a genuine value.

The practical fix is reframing and sequencing, not elimination: choosing deadlines tied to real motivations, avoiding overlapping self-imposed pressures, and deliberately building recovery gaps to prevent burnout.
quotes: Manufactured urgency can lead to burnout, mainly because you set a deliberately made-up deadline that has no natural ending. If you don't have an alarm to tell you when to stop, then damage is around the corner.
The problem with manufactured urgency as it is usually practiced is that we disguise controlled motivation (do it or else) as autonomous motivation (I don't want to do it, but I want the outcome).
I needed to perform because I wanted to keep being the smart kid, as if my identity were merely tied to results.

Not only that, but for animals, stress stops after the threat has gone away. We have gotten used to keeping our alarm on. The stress, the threat, never really leaves our heads. This eventually builds up and can become chronic if untreated.
Prioritizing and leaving space between finishing one milestone and starting something new gives your brain the rest it needs to avoid burnout.

Once you assess the situation and decide, you can enforce the deadlines. For this, motivation is key: focus on how what you need to do aligns with what you want to do, rather than on what you would lose if you don't do it.
